subject: backend
question: Does every connected user receive every chat message?

artifact.code:
connections: set[WebSocket] = set()

@app.websocket("/chat")
async def chat(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    connections.add(ws)
    async for msg in ws.iter_text():
        for c in connections:
            await c.send_text(msg)

# Deployment: 3 replicas behind a load balancer.

ai_claim: Yes. Each message is sent to every connection in the connections set, which holds all connected users.

ai_solution.text: Each new WebSocket is added to connections.
connections contains every connected user.
Incoming messages are sent to every connection in the set.
So every user receives every message.

failure.misconception: Forgetting that each replica has its own memory
failure.explanation: connections is a variable inside one process. With 3 replicas, each holds only the users the load balancer routed to it, so a message reaches roughly a third of the users. Cross-instance broadcast needs a shared channel such as Redis pub/sub (or a message broker) that every replica subscribes to.
failure.why_convincing: On a single local server, every user really is in the same set.

canonical_solution: No: each replica has its own connections set, so messages reach only users on the same replica. Publish messages through Redis pub/sub and have each replica forward them.

valid_evidence.summary: Two users routed to different replicas cannot see each other's messages.
Process memory is not shared between replicas; cross-instance fan-out needs an external channel.

counterexamples: A user on replica A never sees messages sent by a user on replica B.

hints.text: Count how many connections sets exist in production.
Step 2 says one set holds every user.
Each replica is a separate process with its own memory.
Connect two users that land on different replicas.
Step 2 is wrong: each replica has its own set. Use Redis pub/sub to broadcast across replicas.

repair: Publish every message to a Redis channel; each replica subscribes and sends to its own connections.
debrief: Anything kept in process memory - connection lists, sessions, rate-limit counters - silently splits when you scale out. Real-time features need a shared backplane.

subject: backend
question: Will the operations dashboard keep showing live orders all day?
ai_claim: Yes. A WebSocket is a persistent connection, so once it is open, orders keep arriving for as long as the page is open.

ai_solution.text: The page opens a WebSocket to the live-orders endpoint.
WebSocket connections are persistent.
The connection stays open as long as the page is open.
So orders keep arriving all day.

failure.explanation: Persistent means 'not per request', not 'permanent'. Deploys restart the server, load balancers close idle connections, laptops sleep and Wi-Fi changes. When the socket closes, nothing reconnects, so the dashboard silently stops updating while still looking live. Handle onclose by reconnecting with backoff, and re-fetch missed orders.
failure.why_convincing: During a short test nothing interrupts the connection.

canonical_solution: No: the connection will drop (deploys, idle timeouts, network changes) and there is no reconnect logic. Reconnect with backoff and resynchronise state.

valid_evidence.summary: Restart the server: the dashboard stops receiving orders and never recovers.
A load balancer's 60-second idle timeout closes a quiet connection.

counterexamples: After a deploy, the dashboard shows no new orders.

hints.text: List events that can close a long-lived connection.
Step 3 assumes the connection lasts as long as the page.
Networks, proxies and deploys close connections; clients must reconnect.
Restart the server while the dashboard is open.
Step 3 is wrong: connections drop and nothing reconnects. Add reconnection with backoff.

repair: On close, reconnect with exponential backoff and fetch any orders missed while disconnected.
debrief: Real-time clients must assume the connection will fail. Reconnection, backoff and catching up on missed events are part of the feature, not polish.

subject: backend
question: Is the AI right that this detects clients that vanished without closing the connection (for example, a phone that lost signal) within about 30 seconds?

artifact.code:
# Server sends a ping every 20 s; a client that has not answered
# with a pong within 10 s is considered dead and its socket is closed.
async def heartbeat(ws):
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(20)
        try:
            await asyncio.wait_for(ws.ping(), timeout=10)
        except (asyncio.TimeoutError, ConnectionClosed):
            await ws.close()
            connections.discard(ws)
            return

ai_claim: Yes. A vanished client cannot answer the ping, so within 20 seconds the next ping is sent and 10 seconds later it times out; the socket is then closed and removed.

ai_solution.text: A client that loses signal sends no close frame, so the server still thinks it is connected.
At most 20 seconds later the server sends a ping.
No pong arrives, so after 10 more seconds wait_for times out.
The server closes the socket and removes it: detection within about 30 seconds.

canonical_solution: Correct. Without heartbeats, a half-open TCP connection can look alive for a very long time. The ping/pong cycle bounds detection time at about the ping interval plus the timeout.

valid_evidence.summary: last pong at t = 0 -> ping at t <= 20 -> timeout at t <= 30 -> close and discard
TCP does not report a silently vanished peer promptly; application-level heartbeats are needed.

hints.text: Work out the worst-case timing.
Step 3 depends on the ping going unanswered.
Half-open connections are detected only by sending something and expecting a reply.
Add the ping interval and the timeout.
This solution is correct. Worst case 20 + 10 = 30 seconds to detect and clean up. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Heartbeats turn 'connected' into something the server verifies. They also keep idle connections alive through proxies with idle timeouts.

subject: backend
question: Is the AI right that Server-Sent Events are enough for pushing stock updates to browsers, and that the browser reconnects automatically with the last event id?
ai_claim: Yes. Updates only flow from server to browser, which SSE handles over plain HTTP. EventSource reconnects automatically after a drop and sends a Last-Event-ID header with the last id it saw, so the server can resume.

ai_solution.text: Stock updates are one-way: server to browser.
SSE streams events over a normal HTTP response.
EventSource reconnects automatically when the connection drops.
On reconnect it sends Last-Event-ID, set from the id: field, so the server can send what was missed.

canonical_solution: Correct. For one-way push, SSE is simpler than WebSockets and has reconnection and resumption built in. The server must still use Last-Event-ID to replay missed events.

valid_evidence.summary: HTML Living Standard: EventSource reconnects automatically and sends the Last-Event-ID header.
Kill the connection: DevTools shows a new request to /stock/stream with Last-Event-ID set.

hints.text: Check which direction the data flows.
Step 4 depends on the id: field in each event.
SSE is one-way, with built-in reconnection and resume support.
Drop the connection and inspect the reconnect request.
This solution is correct. SSE fits one-way updates and resumes with Last-Event-ID. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Choose the simplest transport that fits the direction of the data. SSE covers most 'live update' features, and its reconnection behaviour is standardised.

subject: backend
question: If a notification is published while the user's phone is briefly offline, will the user receive it after reconnecting?

artifact.code:
async def notify(user_id, message):
    await broker.publish(f"user:{user_id}", message)

# Each connected socket subscribes to its user's channel.
# The broker's configuration and any message storage are not shown.

ai_claim: Yes. The message is published to the user's channel, so it is delivered when the user's socket subscribes again.

ai_solution.text: notify publishes to the user's channel.
The user's socket is disconnected at that moment.
The channel keeps the message until a subscriber appears.
After reconnecting, the user receives it.

missing_information: Whether the broker stores messages for absent subscribers. Plain Redis pub/sub is fire-and-forget: a message published with no subscriber is lost. Redis Streams, Kafka, or a persistent queue keep it and can replay it on reconnect. The broker type and configuration are not shown.
resolving_scenarios: Redis pub/sub: nobody is subscribed at publish time, so the message is dropped and never delivered.
Redis Streams or a durable queue with the client resuming from its last id: the message is delivered after reconnecting.
canonical_solution: It depends on the broker's delivery semantics, which are not given. Step 3 assumes the channel stores messages.

valid_evidence.summary: With Redis PUBLISH, a message sent while no one is subscribed returns 0 receivers and is lost.

counterexamples: With plain pub/sub the notification is lost.

hints.text: Ask what the broker does with a message when nobody is listening.
Step 3 states a property of the broker.
Pub/sub systems differ: some drop messages without subscribers, others persist them.
Compare Redis pub/sub with Redis Streams.
Step 3 assumes persistence. Plain pub/sub drops the message; a durable stream delivers it. It cannot be decided.

repair: Name the broker; for guaranteed delivery, store notifications (a stream or table) and replay them on reconnect.
debrief: 'Published' does not mean 'delivered'. Delivery guarantees - at-most-once, at-least-once, retained or not - are properties of the broker, and they decide what happens to offline users.
